en: Now I tweaked this essential demo here,

file because Bun can of course be used to
build web servers, to build web applications

use cases, though you can of course also use
Bun to build utility tools, CLIs and you'll

counter.
I got a placeholder here for the actual

the counter and those buttons simply submit
the form. So no JavaScript, no client-side
JavaScript involved, just a good old website
with a form inside and that
And then in index.ts, we got a lot going on,
but most importantly, we got bun.serve. And
that is one of the new APIs Bun offers.
As mentioned, it has that Node.js
compatibility and you can just run your
Node.js app with Bun. You can build your
Node and Express app or whatever you're
doing and run it with Bun. But
you can also switch to the Bun native APIs
to have better ergonomics, potentially
better performance.
And Bun serve is one of those native APIs.
By just calling bun.serve
and then configuring your server with a
JavaScript object you pass to it, but by
just running bun serve, you start a web
server that listens on port 3000 by default,
though you can change that with the port
setting here if you want to,
if you run that file.
So if I bun run,
source index.ts here,
you see my server is now up and running on
port 3000. And as long as this process here
is running, that server will be up and
running. We can quit it with Ctrl+C, of
course, to stop it.
But if it is running,
we can visit localhost:3000 to see this
application. And there I can press these
buttons to change the counter.
Now, how is that counter change handled?
Well, not in the index.html file. As I
mentioned, I got no client-side JavaScript
code in there. Instead, I got that form
that's submitted when I hit those buttons.
And we're handling this form submission here
in index.ts. So here in index.ts, we're
doing a couple of things. We got Bun serve
as mentioned, bringing up that server, but
we, for example, also got this import. This
is not something you could do in just
Node.js because here I'm importing an HTML
file, not a TypeScript, not a JavaScript
file, an HTML file.
This is a Bun feature. You can import HTML
files into your TypeScript files as well.
And I'm doing this to use this HTML file as
a template which I wanna dynamically render
and then serve through that Bun server.
So in that serve
configuration object here, we're not just
setting up a port, but instead we have a
fetch method,
an async fetch method.
And that is simply one method, a very
important method you can add to this
configuration object that you pass to serve
because it's this fetch method fetch method,
and it must be named fetch, that tells Bun
what to do for incoming requests,
which is why fetch also receives such an
incoming request.
This is the request received by that Bun
server you spun up. So fetch is the method
you add to control what happens for those
incoming requests.
In this case here, I'm extracting the URL
using the URL class here, which you may know
from browser-side, client-side JavaScript,
because Bun does not just have that built-in
Node.js compatibility and its own extra
APIs, but it also has broad support for many
general web standards and APIs you may know
from the browser, like this URL class, which
you can just use without problems in your
Bun code as well.
And here I'm using it to access the request
URL. So the request we're getting here is an
object of type request, which by the way is
also an API you could also use in the
browser.
And that request object has a URL property.
We now wrap that or convert that into a URL
object.
And that URL object then has utility
properties and methods, for example, the
pathname property, which allows us to find
out which path was in that URL.
The path, of course, is the part after the
domain. So in this case, if there's nothing,
it's just slash.
Typing a slash here is the equivalent to
typing nothing.
So in this check here, we check if the path
is just slash. So if we entered just the
domain and then nothing, essentially.
And we check the request method, if it's a
GET request. And in that case, we know that
we wanna return the HTML file which we
imported, but
not just that HTML file. Keep in mind that
has that weird placeholder in there to
render the actual counter value. And that
counter value is managed here on our server.
I got a counter variable
and I changed that variable down here. I'll
get back to that code. But then I return a
new response here for this GET route where
we wanna serve the site.
And I take the HTML template
which is just the imported HTML here.
And I replace this count placeholder, I look
for it programmatically in the imported HTML
code and I replace it with the current
counter value
converted to a string.
And that is then sent back as an HTML
response.
But this app does not just support
GET requests. We got a form and this form
uses a POST request for submission.
So therefore in index.ts, we also have that
other route where we also check for being on
the root route. But if the request method
then is POST, we use the formData method on
that incoming request. And even though it's
shown as deprecated here in my IDE, this is
the official way of extracting the formData
of an incoming request according to the Bun
docs.
And this formData then holds the submitted
value of that form. Now this form has no
input fields, but it has 2 buttons and each
button has its own value attached. The name
of each button is action, but the value is
different. It's decrement or increment. And
therefore in index.ts, we get hold of that
action value.
Again, action is the name of these buttons.
So we get hold of the submitted value and
the value then is either increment or
decrement as mentioned, and we update the
counter variable accordingly.
And then we redirect here with
response.redirect. We redirect to the root
route so that this route gets triggered and
we output the updated counter.
That's what's happening here. And most of
that code is not very Bun-specific. We're
using standard web APIs here and standard
JavaScript logic, but we're doing all that
in that special async fetch method here in
that Bun serve object. And that is how you
can use Bun native features to build a basic
web server.
